analogy.p: Think of each subprogram as a recipe card pinned in a kitchen. The head chef (the main program) does not explain how to make a sauce every time; she just says 'make sauce' and hands over the ingredients. The ingredients are the arguments, the blanks on the card the parameters, and a function-style recipe returns a finished dish to the table while a procedure-style job, like 'wipe the counter', returns nothing. Items chopped on a cook's own board are local variables, whereas the ingredients on the shared central shelf are globals. It breaks down because a real chef can improvise and use any ingredient, whereas a subprogram can only work with the data passed in and the variables it is allowed to see.

bullets: A subprogram = a named block of code that performs a task; it only runs when it is **called**.
The two types in the specification are **procedures** and **functions**.
Defining a subprogram only **writes** it; nothing happens until the program **calls** it by name.
A subprogram can be called **many times**, from different places, with different data.
Subprograms are what let programmers use **decomposition**: breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems, each solved by one subprogram.
Built-in routines you have already used (such as len, print, input, int) are subprograms written by someone else.
core.p: A **subprogram** is a named, self-contained block of code that carries out one specific task and can be **called** from anywhere in a program whenever that task is needed. In the J277 course the two kinds are **procedures** and **functions**. Instead of writing the same lines again and again, you write them once, give them a name, and then use the name. This is the key tool for producing **structured code**, where a big problem is split into small, understandable parts.

bullets: **Reuse**: write once, call many times, so there is no repeated code and the program is shorter.
**Readability**: a main program made of well-named calls such as calculateTotal() reads almost like English.
**Easier testing and debugging**: each subprogram can be tested on its own; errors are found in one place.
**Easier maintenance**: to change how something works you edit **one** subprogram and every call benefits.
**Teamwork**: different programmers can write different subprograms at the same time.
**Structured, modular design**: supports top-down design and decomposition, which links to computational thinking.
A subprogram can be **reused in other programs**, saving development time.
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to explain why subprograms are used, so you need clear, specific benefits. The main idea is that code is written **once and reused**, which makes programs shorter and quicker to write, easier to read, easier to test and easier to fix. Because each subprogram does one job, a team can share the work and each part can be tested separately before being combined.

bullets: Structure: procedure name(parameters) ... endprocedure.
Example: procedure greet(name) then print("Hello " + name) then endprocedure.
Calling it: greet("Sam") on a line by itself prints Hello Sam.
A procedure does **not** use a return statement to send a value back.
Use a procedure when you want an **action** (display, write to a file, reset variables) rather than an answer.
A procedure call is a whole statement; you cannot meaningfully write x = greet("Sam") because nothing is returned.
core.p: A **procedure** is a subprogram that performs a task but does **not return a value** to the place it was called from. It might display a message, draw something or update a file, and then simply finish. Procedures are called as a statement on their own line. In the OCR reference language a procedure is written between the words procedure and endprocedure, with the name and any parameters on the first line.

bullets: Structure: function name(parameters) ... return value ... endfunction.
Example: function add(a, b) then return a + b then endfunction.
Calling it: total = add(3, 4) stores **7** in total; print(add(3, 4)) displays 7.
The **return** statement ends the function immediately; any code after it in that function is not run.
The returned value has a data type (integer, string, Boolean...) and the caller must use it sensibly.
If you call a function but do not store or output the result, the returned value is **lost**.
Use a function when the calling code needs a **result** to carry on calculating.
core.p: A **function** is a subprogram that **returns a value** to the part of the program that called it. When the function reaches its **return** statement it stops and sends the value back, and the call itself is then replaced by that value. Functions are called as part of an expression, for example by assigning the result to a variable or printing it directly. They are used when you need an **answer**, such as a total, an average or a True/False result.

bullets: Function: **returns** a value; called inside an expression (total = add(2, 3)).
Procedure: **does not return** a value; called as a statement (greet("Sam")).
Both can take **parameters**; both are called by name; both help structure code.
Functions use the keyword **return**; procedures do not.
A function used to display text but returning nothing would be a **procedure** in design terms.
In the exam, a 1-mark answer: 'A function returns a value, a procedure does not.'
A 2-mark answer adds an example or says how each is called.
core.h: Procedure or function? The key difference
core.p: The one-line difference examiners want is that a **function returns a value** and a **procedure does not**. Everything else (name, parameters, being called, containing code) is shared. A good way to decide is to ask: does the rest of the program need an answer from this subprogram? If yes, make it a function; if it only needs something to happen, make it a procedure.

bullets: Parameter = the variable name in the **definition**, e.g. a and b in function add(a, b).
Argument = the actual value passed in the **call**, e.g. 3 and 4 in add(3, 4).
Arguments are matched to parameters **by position**: add(3, 4) gives a = 3, b = 4.
The number of arguments must **match** the number of parameters, or an error occurs.
A subprogram can have **zero, one or many** parameters; with zero you still write the brackets.
Parameters act like **local variables** that only exist while the subprogram runs.
Passing values in via parameters is better than relying on global variables, because the subprogram is **self-contained**.
In GCSE answers many students use 'parameter' for both; try to use 'argument' for the value in the call.
core.p: A **parameter** is a variable named in the subprogram's definition that receives data when the subprogram is called. The actual value you give at the call is called the **argument**. Parameters make a subprogram **flexible**: the same code can be run with different data each time. When the subprogram is called, the arguments are matched to the parameters in **order**, so the first argument goes into the first parameter, and so on.

bullets: return a + b sends back the sum of the two parameters.
A function returning a Boolean can be used directly in an IF: if isValid(age) then.
The function call can be used anywhere a value is allowed: total = add(2, 3) * 2 gives 10.
A function can be **nested** in a call: double(double(3)) first gives 6, then 12.
A function stops at the first return it reaches, so a return inside an IF can end it early.
If the question asks 'what value is returned', give the **value**, not the code.
Return values let one subprogram feed its answer into another, which is how programs are built from small parts.
core.p: The **return value** is the data a function sends back to the code that called it. The return statement picks the value, the function ends, and the calling line receives the value. You can return a number, a string or a Boolean, and the value can be an expression such as a * b or the result of a test such as score >= 50. A function returns exactly **one** value in the J277 course, though that value could be a more complex structure.

bullets: Step 1: the call is reached and execution jumps to the subprogram.
Step 2: arguments are assigned to parameters.
Step 3: the subprogram's code runs top to bottom.
Step 4: the function sends back its return value (a procedure just ends).
Step 5: execution continues at the point where the subprogram was called.
Subprograms can call **other** subprograms, and a subprogram can even call itself (recursion, beyond GCSE).
Define a subprogram **before** the line that calls it when the language requires it.
core.h: Calling a subprogram and the flow of control
core.p: When a subprogram is called, the program **jumps** from the calling line to the start of the subprogram, copies the arguments into the parameters, runs the subprogram's lines in order, and then **returns** to the line after the call (a function also brings back its value). Understanding this order is essential for tracing code. The definition on its own does not run, so a subprogram that is never called does nothing.

bullets: Scope of a local variable = **only within the subprogram** where it is declared.
It exists only **while the subprogram is running**; its memory is freed afterwards.
Trying to use it outside the subprogram causes an **error** (the variable does not exist there).
Two subprograms can each have a local variable called total; they are completely separate.
Using local variables avoids **accidental changes** to data elsewhere, so code is safer and easier to debug.
Local variables use memory only when needed, so they are **efficient**.
core.p: A **local variable** is a variable declared **inside** a subprogram. It is created when the subprogram runs and **disappears when it finishes**, and it can only be used inside that subprogram. Parameters are treated as local too. Because local variables are invisible from outside, two different subprograms can use the same variable name without interfering with each other.

bullets: Scope of a global variable = **the whole program**, including inside subprograms.
It lasts for the **entire run** of the program.
Any subprogram that changes it affects the rest of the program, causing **unexpected side effects**.
Two subprograms using the same global may interfere with each other, making bugs hard to find.
Globals make a subprogram **less self-contained** and harder to reuse in another program.
Good practice: use **local variables and parameters** by default; use a global only when really necessary.
Constants (values that never change, like VAT rate) are a safe kind of global.
core.p: A **global variable** is declared in the main program, outside any subprogram, and can be seen and changed by **every part** of the program. It exists for the whole time the program runs. Global variables are handy for values needed everywhere, such as a game score, but they are risky because any subprogram can change them, which makes errors hard to trace.

bullets: Local: declared inside a subprogram; exists while it runs; used only there.
Global: declared in the main program; exists for the whole program; used anywhere.
Same name local and global are **different variables** in different scopes.
A change to a local variable does not change a global of the same name.
Benefits of local: avoids clashes, saves memory, easier testing. Drawback of global: can be changed anywhere.
If you are asked to 'explain why local variables are better', give: **fewer unintended changes** and **easier debugging**.
Passing data through parameters and return values replaces most uses of globals.
core.p: **Scope** means the part of the program where a variable can be used. Local variables have a small scope (one subprogram) while global variables have a big scope (everywhere). Exam questions often show code and ask what is output, so you must decide which variable the code is using. If a subprogram has a local variable with the same name as a global one, the subprogram uses its own local copy and the global value stays unchanged.

bullets: Top-down design: start with the whole problem, split into sub-problems, write a subprogram for each.
Use descriptive names such as calculateArea, not x1; this improves **readability**.
Keep each subprogram **short and focused** on a single task.
Add **comments** to explain purpose, parameters and return value.
Use **indentation** inside subprograms so the structure is clear.
Reuse existing subprograms rather than copying and pasting code, which spreads errors.
This links to the 'Producing robust programs' topic: maintainability and testing.
core.h: Structured programming and good subprogram design
core.p: **Structured programming** means building a program from clear, separate parts using sequence, selection, iteration and subprograms, rather than one long block. Good subprograms have a **meaningful name**, do **one job**, take the data they need through parameters, and return results instead of changing globals. A main program that mostly calls well-named subprograms is quick to read and to maintain.

bullets: Validation function: isValid(age) returns True or False, used in an IF or WHILE.
Calculation function: average(a, b, c) returns the mean, which the main program prints.
Procedure for output: showMenu() prints the options each time it is called.
Subprograms can take **arrays** as parameters to process a list of values.
A subprogram can read from or write to a **file** and return whether it succeeded.
Return values can be stored in **variables** for later use or in a data structure.
Input is usually done in the main program or a dedicated procedure, and the result passed on as arguments.
core.h: Using subprograms with input, output and data
core.p: Subprograms are used in nearly every programming task: validating input, calculating, searching a list or printing results. A typical pattern is a function that takes values in as parameters, calculates, and returns a result that the main program prints. This separates the **calculation** from the **display**, which makes the code easier to test because you can check the returned value without needing a keyboard or screen.

bullets: Write the **parameters** with their starting values at the call.
Update local variables as each line runs; they vanish after the subprogram ends.
At a return, note the **value returned** and carry it to the calling line.
Keep main program variables separate from local ones, even if they have the same name.
Nested calls are worked out **from the inside out**: double(double(3)) = double(6) = 12.
Check the output order carefully when a procedure prints during its run.
State the final output exactly as it would appear, including spaces and any text.
core.p: Tracing means working through code by hand, line by line, recording variable values. With subprograms, keep track of **which** variables belong to the main program and **which** are local to the subprogram. When a call happens, write down the parameter values; when a return happens, write down the value sent back and where it goes. A trace table with one column per variable and a note of the call is a safe method.

bullets: Step 1: **function or procedure?** Does the caller need a value back?
Step 2: choose a clear **name** and list the **parameters** needed.
Step 3: write the body using calculations, IF statements or loops.
Step 4: for a function, add **return**; for a procedure, do not return a value.
Step 5: finish with endfunction or endprocedure (OCR reference language).
Step 6: write the **call** with suitable arguments and use or print the result.
Step 7: check the function returns the right data type on every path.
core.h: Writing a subprogram from a description
core.p: To write a subprogram in an exam, follow a repeatable method. Decide if it needs to return an answer (function) or just perform an action (procedure), name it sensibly, identify the data it needs as parameters, write the body, and make sure a function ends with a return. Then write the line that calls it. Marks are given for the correct header, correct parameters, correct body logic, correct return, and a correct call.

bullets: **Computational thinking**: decomposition = breaking a problem into subprograms; abstraction = using a subprogram without knowing how it works.
**Robust programs**: validation routines and maintainability (comments, naming) are often written as subprograms.
**Testing**: individual subprograms can be tested separately with normal, boundary and erroneous data.
**Arrays and records**: can be passed into subprograms as parameters.
**Data types and casting**: return values and parameters have data types that must match.
**Algorithms**: searching and sorting are normally coded as subprograms that return a result or a sorted list.
**Random numbers and string handling**: built-in subprograms such as random and len are used inside your own.
core.p: Subprograms connect to many other areas. They put decomposition and abstraction from computational thinking into practice, they carry out the validation and testing needed for robust programs, and they work with arrays, records and files. Understanding scope also helps you explain how memory is used, because local variables only exist while the subprogram runs.

exam: 1 mark 'Give one difference between a function and a procedure': 'A function returns a value, a procedure does not.' Say who returns what.
2 mark 'Describe a function/procedure': 'A named block of code that performs a task' + 'can be called many times / returns a value (function)'.
'Explain why subprograms are used' (2 to 3 marks): give a benefit AND a reason, e.g. 'Code can be reused, so it does not need to be rewritten, which makes the program shorter and quicker to write'.
Benefit words to use: reusable, readable, easier to test/debug, easier to maintain, teamwork, shorter, structured.
'Give two differences between local and global variables' (2 marks): scope (one subprogram vs whole program) and lifetime (while subprogram runs vs whole program).
'Explain one reason for using local variables' (2 marks): 'They cannot be changed by other parts of the program, so there are fewer unintended errors and it is easier to debug'.
Trace questions: write parameter values at the call, track locals, and note the returned value. Give the final output exactly.
Write-the-code questions (up to 6 marks): header with correct name and parameters, correct logic, correct return, endfunction/endprocedure, and a correct call.
For a function, always check there is a return on every possible path, and that the call uses the returned value.
Command words: State = short fact; Describe = what it is/does; Explain = give a reason using 'because/so'; Write = produce code.
Do not just say 'it is easier' or 'it saves time' without saying why; examiners reward the reason (reuse, no repetition, one place to change).

mistakes.r: A function returns a value to the caller; a procedure does not return a value.
mistakes.w: A function and a procedure are the same thing.

mistakes.r: The values in the call are arguments; parameters are the variable names in the definition that receive them.
mistakes.w: Parameters are the values you type when calling the subprogram.

mistakes.r: A local variable can only be used inside the subprogram in which it is declared.
mistakes.w: Local variables can be used anywhere in the program.

mistakes.r: Globals can be changed from anywhere, causing unexpected errors; local variables and parameters are better practice.
mistakes.w: Global variables are better because they can be used everywhere.

mistakes.r: Subprograms make code reusable, shorter, easier to read, test and maintain; they do not necessarily speed it up.
mistakes.w: Subprograms make the program run faster.

mistakes.r: A subprogram only runs when it is called.
mistakes.w: Defining a function makes it run.

mistakes.r: The returned value must be stored in a variable or output, e.g. total = add(3, 4).
mistakes.w: Forgetting to use the returned value: add(3, 4) on its own line.

mistakes.r: The function ends at the return statement, so later lines in that function are not executed.
mistakes.w: Writing code after a return statement and expecting it to run.

mistakes.r: They are separate variables; the subprogram uses its local copy and the global is unchanged.
mistakes.w: Local and global variables with the same name are the same variable.

mistakes.r: The number and order of arguments must match the parameters.
mistakes.w: Using a subprogram without the right number of arguments.

summary: The spec asks you to use subprograms (procedures and functions) to produce structured code, including parameters, return values, and local and global variables. You must explain the difference between a function and a procedure, trace and write subprograms, and justify why they are used. This matters because every substantial program is built from reusable, testable subprograms.

terms.d: A named block of code that performs a specific task and can be called from elsewhere in a program.
A subprogram that performs a task but does not return a value.
A subprogram that returns a value to the part of the program that called it.
A statement that runs a subprogram by using its name, with any arguments in brackets.
A variable named in a subprogram's definition that receives a value when the subprogram is called.
The actual value passed to a subprogram when it is called.
The data a function sends back to the code that called it.
A variable declared inside a subprogram that can only be used within that subprogram and exists only while it runs.
A variable declared in the main program that can be used anywhere in the program for as long as it runs.
The part of a program in which a variable can be accessed.
Writing programs from clear, separate parts using sequence, selection, iteration and subprograms.
Breaking a problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.
Splitting a program into separate modules or subprograms that each perform one task.
Being able to use the same code again in different places or programs without rewriting it.
The statement in a function that sends a value back and ends the function.
How easily a program can be understood, corrected and updated.

Trace the following and state what is displayed.
function double(n)
  return n * 2
endfunction
x = double(double(3))
print(x) [3]

worked.ans: Subprograms can be reused: a task such as validating input is written once and called whenever needed, so the programmer does not have to repeat code and the program is shorter. They make the program easier to test and maintain: each subprogram can be tested on its own, and if a change is needed only the one subprogram has to be edited, not every place the code was copied.
worked.q: Explain two benefits of using subprograms when writing a large program. [4]
